context.problemStatement:
Implement the `Lambda` case of `eval`. An anonymous function `fn(x) { ... }`
evaluates to a function value. Nothing in its body is evaluated until it is
called, so this case never returns an error. Build a `VFunc(UserFn(...))` whose
name is `"lambda"` (used in error messages) and whose parent is the environment
in which this function was *defined*, not the one in which it will be called. This
is what lets a function use the names around it, even after the call that created it
has returned.

```
// In eval:
    Lambda(params, body) ->
      // YOUR CODE HERE (replace the code below)
      Error(errors.NotImplemented(
        "Lambda("
        <> string.inspect(params)
        <> ", "
        <> string.inspect(body)
        <> ")",
      ))
```

Run the tests:

```
gleam test -- q8
```

targets.claim: Student can explain why their Lambda case never returns an error even when the body of the anonymous function uses an unbound name, and when such an error would appear instead.

probes.question: In your `Lambda(params, body)` arm, why does evaluating an expression like `fn(x) { missing_name }` immediately return `Ok` without raising an unbound variable error, and at what point would an error for `missing_name` actually happen?
probes.reason: Directly asks why evaluating a lambda never fails on undefined names and pinpoints when the evaluation of its body occurs instead.

probes.question: Your `Lambda` arm simply constructs `Ok(VFunc(UserFn("lambda", params, body, env)))` without calling `eval` on `body`. Why doesn't it check if `body` is valid right now, and when does `body` actually get evaluated?
probes.reason: Provides an alternative phrasing referencing their exact returned value and asks for the explanation of deferred evaluation.
